lessons.title: This week in {{league}}
lessons.objective: Get the week's key games and context for this week's action.

payload.prompt: This week's {{league}} schedule features multiple playoff-race implications. Why does early seeding matter?

options.text: Seeds determine playoff matchups; every win shifts seeding race.
Seeds determine home-court advantage in playoffs, which is worth a few points.
Early seeding sets the tone for the rest of the season.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Seeding means playoff spots and home court. Games now matter for spring.
explanation.incorrect: Week-to-week games shift seeds and playoff positioning. Seeding determines playoff matchups and home court.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: Our team plays three games this week and every one is against a contender.

options.text: A brutal schedule against strong teams tests whether they can compete with the best.
Easy wins against contenders are guaranteed.
Playing good teams hurts their playoff chances.
Winning does not matter against contenders.

payload.translation: She means this week is a big test. Wins against contenders boost playoff positioning.

followUps.line: Think they can win most of them?
followUps.why: Good: invites her to assess their roster against elite teams.
Valid: acknowledges the difficulty without predicting outcomes.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Playing contenders on the road is hard. Wins here prove readiness.

payload.prompt: If {{team}} splits this week's games, how does that affect their seeding race?

options.text: One win and one loss keeps them steady in the standings.
Splits against contenders show they can trade wins.
Every game matters; splitting wastes opportunities against elite teams.

explanation.correct: Right. In a tight seeding race, beating contenders lifts you; splitting does not move you much.
explanation.incorrect: Close seeds mean wins against contenders matter. A split feels neutral but lost ground to direct competitors.

payload.prompt: One game back of eighth seed, three contenders ahead. Go for it or rest?

facts.label: Key players
facts.value: One has a minor injury, playable

facts.label: Playoff odds
facts.value: Win all three: 85% chance to make playoffs

options.label: Play full strength, go for it.
options.consequence: Winning three straight secures playoff position. The reward justifies the risk.

options.label: Sit the injured player; be cautious.
options.consequence: Safer approach if you value continuity over seeding wins. But playoff odds drop.

payload.expertNote: Late-season intensity against contenders is a playoff preview. Go all-in unless injury risk is severe.

payload.prompt: NBA teams play {{games-per-week}} games per week on average during the regular season.
payload.template: NBA teams play {{games-per-week}} games per week on average during the regular season.

explanation.correct: Right. Most weeks have 2-4 games; average is about three.
explanation.incorrect: NBA schedule spreads games across the week. Most teams play 3 games per week on average.

lessons.title: {{team}}: game preview
lessons.objective: Preview {{team}}'s next game and what to watch for.

payload.prompt: {{team}} plays a back-to-back this week. What should you watch for?

options.text: Bench unit performance; starters get extra rest on day two.
Energy levels and pace; second nights fatigue the team.
The coach's rotation shrinks; fewer players get heavy minutes.

explanation.correct: All three happen. Back-to-backs change everything: rotation, pace, and who plays.
explanation.incorrect: Back-to-backs are brutal. Watch for rotation changes, bench stepping up, and tired defense.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: This matchup is perfect for {{player}}. Their defense is slow.

options.text: She is identifying a mismatch: the opponent's slow defense suits {{player}}'s speed.
She is insulting the opponent.
The matchup is bad for {{player}}.
Speed has no impact on defense.

payload.translation: She means the opponent's weak perimeter defense is a gift for a quick player like {{player}}.

followUps.why: Good: you are thinking about whether he exploits the matchup.

followUps.line: That defense is not great anyway.
followUps.why: Valid observation about their general struggles.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Mismatch-hunting is key: when the other team's defender cannot keep up, a player attacks it.

payload.prompt: Your team is on a four-game road trip. Tonight is game two. Rotation strategy?

facts.label: Trip
facts.value: Four games in six nights, two more after tonight

options.label: Rest starters now, lean on bench.
options.consequence: Conserve energy for the final two games. Bench gets valuable minutes.
considerations: This game is winnable with bench.
Save the stars for critical games.

options.label: Play to win; go full strength.
options.consequence: Win now, handle fatigue later. But risky if key players get hurt.

payload.expertNote: Four-game trips are grinding. Winners rest strategically against non-elite teams early in the trip.

payload.prompt: {{team}} announced a late-game injury update. What should you check before game time?

options.text: The league's official injury report and the team's public statements.
Social media rumors and player hints.
The coach's game-day practice notes.

explanation.correct: Official sources only. The league injury report is the truth.
explanation.incorrect: Stick to official reports. Social media is speculation; rumors are not facts.

payload.title: Game preview talk
payload.setting: She is excited and nervous about tonight's game. You want to talk about what might happen.

exchanges.theirMessage: I hope they win tonight. Our playoff chances depend on it.

replies.text: What is your team's biggest edge against this opponent?
replies.theirResponse: Good question. We are way faster on the wings.
replies.coachNote: You asked about their team's strength, inviting analysis.
You agreed but did not add anything new to the talk.

exchanges.theirMessage: Do you think {{player}} will go off tonight?

replies.text: Depends on whether their defense can keep up. Does he usually score against this team?
replies.theirResponse: He is always better at home. We are on the road, though.
replies.coachNote: You connected individual skill to matchup; she gave you more info.

replies.text: He always scores. That is what he does.
replies.theirResponse: True, but some teams can slow him down.

payload.closingNote: Game previews are about matchups and momentum. Talk about edges and concerns.

lessons.title: Why is everyone talking about this?
lessons.objective: Decode the week's biggest basketball story and why fans care.

payload.prompt: A star player just signed a supermax contract extension. Why is that huge news?

options.text: It costs the team a ton of cap space; they cannot trade or sign freely.
It signals the player wants to stay, shaping the team's future.
It immediately affects playoff seeding and matchups.

explanation.correct: Right. Supermax contracts lock in players and cap space. That shapes team building.
explanation.incorrect: Player signings matter for cap and chemistry. A supermax signals commitment and limits flexibility.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: The trade deadline is two weeks away and nobody knows what to expect.

options.text: Trades are unpredictable; teams make moves based on health, seeding and opportunity.
Trade deadline trades are always quiet.
All contenders make the same trades.
Trades do not happen at the deadline anymore.

payload.translation: She means deadline trades are a wild card. Who moves where is genuinely uncertain.

followUps.line: Think your team will do anything?
followUps.why: Invites her to predict her team's moves based on their situation.
Fair observation: trades do look surprising until the context is clear.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Trade deadlines create buzz because moves are real and impact playoff positioning.

payload.prompt: A team fired their coach mid-season. Is that a reset or a sign of trouble?

facts.label: Record
facts.value: 35 wins, 25 losses; still in playoff race

facts.label: Interim
facts.value: An assistant takes over; knows the team

options.label: It is a reset; could spark a run.
options.consequence: Fresh coaching can fix culture issues. The interim coach has respect.

options.label: It signals locker room dysfunction.
options.consequence: True that mid-season firings indicate problems. But a change sometimes solves it.
considerations: Sometimes it is just bad culture.

payload.expertNote: Mid-season coaching changes succeed when locker room was the problem, not talent.

payload.prompt: A league rule change is announced for next season. Why do fans care now?

options.text: It might affect playoff strategy and team composition immediately.
It gives months of time to adapt; fans follow it for discussion.
It has no impact on this season, so fans focus on next year.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Rule changes announced now affect team planning and fan debate.
explanation.incorrect: Rule changes shape how teams think about trades and draft. Fans follow them because they matter.

lessons.title: Injury report decoder
lessons.objective: Understand injury reports and what they mean for games this week.

payload.prompt: A player is listed as questionable for tonight. What does that mean?

options.text: He will not play; it is a precaution.
He is uncertain to play; a game-time decision.
He will definitely play but is limited.

explanation.correct: Right. Questionable means game-time decision. You find out at warmups.
explanation.incorrect: Questionable is the middle ground: the player might play, but it is uncertain.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: Three players are out tonight. That is a huge opportunity for the bench.

options.text: Missing starters mean role players and bench get more minutes and shots.
Injuries do not affect playing time.
The bench is always ready to start.
Bench players are never good substitutes.

payload.translation: She means injuries create a chance for lesser-known players to step up.

followUps.line: Can the bench actually win without them?
followUps.why: Good: you are thinking about whether depth is real or just depth.
Fair: lighthearted way to root for the reserves.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Injuries are opportunities for backup players. Some rise to the occasion; others do not.

payload.prompt: A star player is listed as out for load management on the second night of a back-to-back.

pairs.text: Smart. Protecting him now keeps him fresh for playoffs.
pairs.why: Load management extends careers. One game is not worth the risk.

pairs.text: Lazy. He should play through; that is what stars do.
pairs.why: Load management is standard now. Preventing injury beats forcing a player through fatigue.

explanation.correct: Load management is strategic. Playing 82 games hurts; rest helps.
explanation.incorrect: Modern stars rest strategically. One back-to-back game is not worth the risk to a long playoff run.

payload.prompt: A team suddenly has four players in health and safety protocols. How does that change tonight's game?

facts.label: Win expectation
facts.value: Was close; now favors the opponent

facts.label: Timing
facts.value: In the middle of a playoff push

options.label: A loss here hurts the seeding race.
options.consequence: Yes. Playing without depth against a full team is a likely loss.
considerations: One game hurts the playoff race.

options.label: Bench players get a chance; could be a surprise.
options.consequence: True that upsets happen. But the odds are tough without your core.

payload.expertNote: Missing multiple rotation players is brutal. Expect to lose, focus on the next week.

payload.prompt: Standard NBA injury statuses are: out, questionable, {{gtdStatus}}, and doubtful.
payload.template: Standard NBA injury statuses are: out, questionable, {{gtdStatus}}, and doubtful.

explanation.correct: Right. Game-time decision (GTD) means the call comes at warmups.
explanation.incorrect: GTD (game-time decision) is when a player's status is confirmed at game warmups.

lessons.title: Standings and seeding race
lessons.objective: Read the standings, understand seeding and where {{team}} stands.

payload.prompt: {{team}} is tied in wins with another team. The tiebreaker goes to {{tiebreaker}}. What matters now?

options.text: Head-to-head record against that team over the season.
Which team won the coin flip to be announced first.
Strength of schedule for remaining games.

explanation.correct: Head-to-head is the first tiebreaker. It is the fairest way to separate teams.
explanation.incorrect: Tiebreakers follow a hierarchy: head-to-head first, then division win %, then conference win %, etc.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: We are right on the edge of the Play-In. One more loss and we are in danger.

options.text: She means being 7th-10th seeds gets a team into the Play-In tournament; slipping lower means Play-In or missing playoffs.
The Play-In is a guaranteed spot in the playoffs.
Seeding does not affect the Play-In.
All teams go through the Play-In.

payload.translation: She is tracking seeding closely. If her team drops, they are in the Play-In gauntlet.

followUps.line: How many games back are you from the six seed?
followUps.why: Good: you are thinking about the gap between Play-In and direct playoff spots.
Valid: even making Play-In is not safe.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: 7-10 seeds make the Play-In. Missing the 6-seed is the line between direct playoffs and Play-In risk.

payload.prompt: {{team}} is three games back of the five seed with eight games left. Make playoffs or rest?

facts.label: Gap
facts.value: Three games back of 5th seed (direct playoff spot)

facts.label: Schedule
facts.value: Mix of strong and weak opponents

options.label: Go all-in to chase the five seed.
options.consequence: Three games in eight is possible. Direct playoffs save energy for playoffs.

options.label: Lock up the nine seed and rest up.
options.consequence: Play-In is winnable. But direct playoffs is safer. Choice depends on health.

payload.expertNote: Close seeding races are decided in the final week. Three games back is close enough to chase.

payload.prompt: In the standings table, tap where to find how many games back {{team}} is from the one seed.
payload.description: A standings table shows seed, team, wins, losses, and games back (GB).

spots.label: Games Back column (GB)
spots.feedback: Right. GB shows the gap between a team and the leader.

spots.label: Wins column
spots.feedback: Wins alone do not show the gap. You need games back to see how close they are.

spots.label: Seed number
spots.feedback: Seed tells you rank but not how far back. Look at GB for distance.

payload.prompt: Why does conference matter in seeding?

options.text: Each conference gets 8 playoff seeds; teams rank within their conference.
Conference champions get a bye to the second round.
Conference rivalries determine playoff matchups.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Seeds 1-8 East, 1-8 West. Conference determines your playoff bracket.
explanation.incorrect: Conferences divide the league. Seeds rank within each conference, determining first-round matchups.

lessons.title: Trades and free agency explainer
lessons.objective: Decode trades, signings and the salary cap impact on team building.

payload.prompt: Your team trades for a player mid-season. What is the benefit?

options.text: Immediate roster upgrade for the playoff push.
The acquired player is always better than who you gave up.
Trades never backfire.

explanation.correct: Right. Mid-season trades add talent for a playoff run. No guarantee of success.
explanation.incorrect: Trades are gambles. You add talent but give up future assets or depth.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: That trade looks bad long-term but makes sense for this year.

options.text: She means the team sacrificed future assets to win now, a valid playoff-push trade-off.
The trade is objectively bad.
All trades help the future.
Trades always look good long-term.

payload.translation: She is recognizing the tension: this trade adds a star now but costs flexibility later.

followUps.line: Does it make you a contender this year?
followUps.why: Good: you are asking if the gamble is worth it now.
Fair assessment that trading future assets is a risk.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Playoff teams often trade future picks or prospects for present talent. It is a valid strategy.

payload.prompt: Your contender is near the salary cap. A star becomes available at the deadline. Trade or pass?

facts.label: Playoff window
facts.value: This is the year; next year is uncertain

facts.label: Trade cost
facts.value: Three good young players and a pick

options.label: Trade for the star now.
options.consequence: Add a superstar in your playoff window. The young players' loss hurts long-term but wins now.

options.label: Pass; keep the young core.
options.consequence: Preserves future but risks wasting your window. A hard choice.

payload.expertNote: Contenders trade young talent for stars. It is a calculated risk when playoffs are now.

payload.prompt: Match salary cap terms to their meanings.

pairs.definition: The spending limit for a team's player salaries; teams over it pay a luxury tax.
A credit from a previous trade allowing a team to absorb a player's salary without counting it.
A second spending threshold above the luxury tax; exceeding it triggers harsher penalties.

distractorDefinitions: A bonus given to players for winning.
A percentage increase in a player's salary each year.

explanation.summary: Cap rules limit spending. Exceptions let teams absorb salary. Aprons add penalties for big spenders.

lessons.title: Playoff series tracker
lessons.objective: Understand playoff seeding, bracket predictions and why every late-season game matters.

payload.prompt: In the playoffs, why does seeding matter so much?

options.text: Seeds determine playoff matchups and home-court advantage throughout the bracket.
Seeds give byes to higher seeds in the first round.
Seeding determines which team wins the championship.

explanation.correct: Right. One plays eight, two plays seven, etc. Home court comes with being the higher seed.
explanation.incorrect: Seeding sets the bracket. First seed hosts game one, travels for game two, etc. Huge advantage.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: If we land the three seed, we might duck the two seed in the first round.

options.text: She means seeding determines matchups; getting three protects against facing the defending champion two seed.
Seeds randomly pair up in the playoffs.
Avoiding tough teams is guaranteed.
Seeds do not affect first-round matchups.

payload.translation: She is thinking about bracket implications. Three seed plays six; two seed plays seven. Avoiding them is lucky.

followUps.line: Who do you think is the second seed?
followUps.why: Good: invites her to name the current threat.

followUps.line: Best record is always the two seed.
followUps.why: Not quite: one seed has best record. But you are thinking about the bracket.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Bracket seeding is rigid: 1 vs 8, 2 vs 7, 3 vs 6, 4 vs 5. Seeding determines path to the Finals.

payload.prompt: {{team}} can clinch the three seed with one win in three games. Conservative or aggressive?

facts.label: Seed
facts.value: Sitting fourth; three seed is within reach

facts.label: Games
facts.value: Three left, mix of strong and weak teams

facts.label: Playoff opponent
facts.value: Three seed faces five seed; four faces six seed

options.label: Play to clinch the three seed.
options.consequence: One win vs. three weaker opponents; sets up an easier first-round matchup.

options.label: Rest key players; accept the four.
options.consequence: Four seed is still first-round home games. Rest helps, but playoff path is tougher.

payload.expertNote: Playoff seeding is worth playing for. One better seed often means an easier first-round opponent.

payload.prompt: Tap the first-round matchup if your team is the three seed and has the best record in the conference.
payload.description: Bracket shows 1 seed vs 8, 2 vs 7, 3 vs 6, 4 vs 5 in the first round.

spots.label: Three seed plays six seed
spots.feedback: Right. Three seed is third-best record; plays sixth seed, the sixth-best.

spots.label: Three seed plays seven seed
spots.feedback: No. Seven plays two seed. Seeds pair symmetrically: 1-8, 2-7, 3-6, 4-5.

spots.label: One seed plays three seed
spots.feedback: No. One plays eight. First-round seeding is fixed.

lessons.title: Awards and All-Star season
lessons.objective: Understand MVP voting, All-Star selections and why awards matter.

payload.prompt: What makes a player an MVP candidate?

options.text: Elite scoring, team success and narrative matter almost equally to voters.
Whoever scores the most points wins MVP.
MVP is always determined by regular-season statistics alone.

explanation.correct: Right. MVP voters balance scoring, efficiency, team record and story. It is subjective.
explanation.incorrect: MVP voting weighs stats but also team wins and narrative. The best scorer does not always win.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: {{player}} is putting up numbers but his team is struggling. That hurts his MVP chances.

options.text: She means MVP voters reward team success; individual stats on losing teams count less.
Individual stats are the only MVP criteria.
Team record does not matter in MVP voting.
All-Star selections and MVP are the same thing.

payload.translation: She is noting the MVP narrative: great stats on bad teams lose to decent stats on great teams.

followUps.line: Can his team make the playoffs?
followUps.why: Good: you are thinking about whether team success can still happen.
Fair opinion, but MVP voters weight team wins.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: MVP voting is not purely statistical. Great players on good teams usually win over stats guys on bad teams.

payload.prompt: Three players are close in MVP voting late in the season. Who do voters pick?

facts.label: Narrative
facts.value: A is a young phenom; B is a veteran leader; C is a role player elevated

options.label: Player B; team success and veteran respect.
options.consequence: First seed and strong narrative. MVP voters reward teams that win.

options.label: Player A; best raw numbers.
options.consequence: A has the highest scoring. Stats matter, but team success usually wins.

payload.expertNote: MVP voters weigh stats and narrative. First seed leading usually means that player's team is winning.

payload.prompt: How is the All-Star Game team selected?

options.text: Fan vote (50%), player vote (25%), coach vote (25%) determines the 12-person roster per conference.
The commissioner selects all All-Stars based on statistics.
Only the best players from the top two seeds make it.

explanation.correct: Right. Fans vote, players vote, coaches vote. All-Star selection is a mix.
explanation.incorrect: All-Star selection is democratic: fan voting, peer voting, and coach input all count.
